title: Snare drum
reference_instrument: Salamander Drumkit snare, 14x6, wires on, overhead microphones (Alexander Holm, CC BY-SA 3.0); the kit copies its sizes, not its materials. The distribution holds one overhead-labelled sample set and does not say whether close-microphone signal is mixed into it, so a line balance measured on it may not be comparable to an overhead-only render
summary: A 14x6 snare from fs-vkplate's one finite-difference solver. It has two tensioned PET heads from a sourced film card, the air between them, a hickory stick from a sourced wood card, and eighteen snare strands pressed up into the resonant head. On the card route each strand is a helical coil of steel music wire. Its geometry is the maker's stated wire diameter, coil outer diameter and pitch, and its stiffness, mass and loss come from two steel cards and the air, not from a recording. The strands' count, spacing and length are declared. Their tension, preload and contact law were adopted in a kit retuning graded against the recording (96ccf8f1b) and are still in use. The strand ends are pinned with no damping, so the lowest coil modes keep their long material decay. The site render is the 3.5 mm grid at 8d757787c, with every strand node on the head node it presses (02b7d8b17). The wires' load now comes on from rest over the settle, so the strike lands on a quiet drum: at most 9.7e-5 Pa in the first 7 ms, where the old start, with the load applied all at once, held a 112 Hz ring of 0.77 Pa. These figures were measured on 2026-10-31. Over the first 250 ms against the recording, the 125 Hz band is 7.7 dB louder, the 63 Hz band is 2.0 dB louder, and the bands from 1 to 8 kHz are 8 to 13 dB weaker. The spectral centroid is 287 Hz against the recording's 1083 Hz, and the share of energy above 1 kHz is 2.2 % against 21 %. Most of these figures are further from the recording than the old start's, and no card value was changed to bring them back. The strongest line in the first 250 ms is now 111 Hz, against the recording's 235.5 Hz. With the old start it was 185 Hz: the 111 Hz line rose 8 dB and the 185 Hz line stayed within 1 dB. The peak is 25.2 Pa, over the 19.2 to 20.8 Pa predicted before the render. The buzz still ends too early, and the ring was not why: the 2 to 16 kHz band is 30 dB below its maximum 100 ms into the file, 95 ms after onset, against 235 ms after onset in the recording. It is already 5 dB under the recording at 30 ms and 7 dB under at 60 ms, then falls 22 dB between 50 and 90 ms to near the recording's wires-off level, where the recording falls 8 dB. The cause is not named. The 2.25 and 9 m/s strikes and the 2.5 mm grid have not been rendered with this start, so the figures that follow are the old start's. At 3.5 and 2.5 mm the 125 Hz band was 4.8 and 7.5 dB louder, the 63 Hz band 1.3 dB quieter and 2.6 dB louder, the bands from 1 to 8 kHz 7 to 11 dB weaker, the centroid 353 and 338 Hz and the share above 1 kHz 2.7 and 3.4 %. Those two grids agreed, so the missing high band was not a grid artifact. The main fall followed the strike speed: at half, full and double speed the band was 15 dB below its maximum at 64, 72 and 157 ms, the order a lift-off threshold predicts. The 30 dB point did not (215, 100 and 185 ms), because at half speed it landed in a tail near 67 dB that lasted to about 200 ms. The presets and the live engine keep the older plain-string wires, which were fitted to a recording and are labelled so, and the GPU renderer refuses a snare with wires on, because its kernel holds a load constant.
physics_present: Batter and resonant heads: tensioned PET film with its own bending stiffness and Berger nonlinearity, from a sourced film card
The exterior radiation load of each head from a baked baffled table, and the viscous boundary layer of the air on both faces of each head
A lumped adiabatic air cavity between the heads, and a radiation resistance on their net volume flow
A hickory stick from a sourced wood card, with a Hertz tip transversely isotropic about the grain

Snare strands on the card route: coils whose bending stiffness combines wire bending and wire torsion over each turn, and whose mass is the wire's, from the steel music-wire card and a spring-moduli card for the shear modulus

Per-mode loss of each coil: the computed thermoelastic loss of the round wire, the card's measured excess bending loss inside its measured band, and the exact linear air drag across and along the wire
One-sided power-law contacts between every strand node and the resonant head, each solved implicitly
A Rayleigh-integral microphone about a metre away, with a floor reflection
physics_missing: Strand-end supports: each strand is pinned at the end plates with no strand-end or cord damping, so the lowest coil modes keep their long material decay. Against the recording the 63 and 125 Hz bands are 2.0 and 7.7 dB louder in the site render. With the old start they were 2.6 and 7.5 dB louder on the 2.5 mm grid, and 1.3 dB quieter and 4.8 dB louder on the 3.5 mm grid

Convergence below 2.5 mm: with the old start, at 4.5 m/s, the 3.5 and 2.5 mm grids agree on when the buzz ends, on each octave's 20 dB fall from 500 Hz to 8 kHz, and on the centroid within 4 %; the 125 Hz band moves 2.8 dB. The 2.5 mm grid has not been run with the landed start, and a 2.0 mm grid has not been run

What ends the buzz: not named. It was not the grid with the old start, and it is not the ring that start left before the strike, because the buzz ends as early without it. At 4.5 m/s the drum's lowest band (100 to 180 Hz) falls 21.5 dB around 35 ms and the buzz follows about 33 ms later. From 100 to 290 ms that band sits at 89 to 90 dB, 5 to 7 dB above the old start's 82 to 85 dB, and the rise is not explained. With the old start the band fell about 23 dB at 4.5 and 9 m/s with the buzz about 25 ms behind it, and at 2.25 m/s it had no such fall: its maximum, 100 dB, was only 11 dB above the ring. In the recording it falls at the same rate at two dynamics, and the buzz outlasts it. All strands share one declared preload and one declared contact loss

The resonant head is heard only through the floor image, not directly. A lumped estimate of both heads and the air between them (pexfp.378, parked) says: if this estimate is right, the current renders overstate each drum's lowest line by 13-17 dB at the overhead
Per-strand tension and preload: one tension and one preload serve every strand. Neither is sourced: both, with the contact law, were adopted in a kit retuning graded against the recording (96ccf8f1b)
The strand count, spacing and length are declared estimates, and the strand-to-head contact law is the retuned one
Wire torsion loss is unmeasured and omitted. The air drag is the linear law, which understates the drag on a rattling wire. The wires' loss is therefore a lower bound
Head film and edge loss: the film card makes no audio-band loss claim, so both are stated unknowns entered as zero
Shell, hoop and rim vibration, and the cavity's own acoustic modes (the cavity is lumped)
The snare is simulated alone, so it does not buzz when another drum is struck
On the preset and live routes the strands are plain strings fitted to a recording (96ccf8f1b), not physics. The GPU route refuses a snare with wires on
